newsitem.title: FRANCE: France can hit 1997 EMU deficit target - OECD.
newsitem.headline: France can hit 1997 EMU deficit target - OECD.

text.p: France will slightly overshoot the 1997 public deficit target required to qualify for European monetary union, but could still hit the threshold, even in its strictist interpretation, with some fine tuning, the OECD says.

The Organisation for Economic Co-Operation and Development said in its semi-annual economic outlook on Thursday it expected France's general government deficit to be 3.2 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) in 1997, above the three percent target laid down in the Maastrict Treaty.
But the Paris-based think-tank added: "The size of the projected slippage is minor and there should be room to cope with any slippage in future budget amendments".

The OECD said its deficit forecast for France diverged from the government forecast of three percent because it expected spending on health to increase at a faster rate than the government had predicted.

It also said the level of French interest rates would need to be set to support an increase in economic growth in 1997 as spending cutbacks alone would not be enough to let France pass the economic fitness test set out in the Maastricht Treaty.
In any case, the Maastricht treaty deficit target is open to more flexible interpretation, even if Germany is pushing for a strict application of the three percent rule.

"The government's success in bringing down the general government deficit to three percent of GDP in 1997 depends not only on the resolute implementation of fiscal consolidation plans, but also on the likely course of interest rates supporting the non-inflation growth of economic activity," the OECD said.
Mass unemployment, the main bugbear of a French government whose popularity is languishing at record lows in opinion polls, looks set to remain a problem, according to the OECD report.
Unemployment is currently at a record 12.6 percent and the OECD forecasters do not expect it to come below 12 percent until the end of 1998, well after the next French general election.

Nevertheless, the OECD was more upbeat about the prospects for growth in 1997 than the French government. It forecast a 2.5 percent increase in GDP, above the government's 2.3 percent forecast, and it predicted growth of 2.6 percent in 1998.
Growth would be boosted by demand for goods from other countries, investment by French companies, higher spending by consumers and more new homes being built, the report said.
It said although output growth has not yet shown clear signs of significant reacceleration the current economic weakness should dissipate progressively.

The OECD was also confident price rises would not accelerate in tandem with any pickup in economic activity because there was still enough productive capacity lying idle which could be used to meet an increase in demand.
"Despite stronger growth, an acceleration in underlying inflation is unlikely because a sizeable output gap will persist," the OECD said in the report.
